test_cases.name: Framework Carousel — produce the content
test_cases.description: User wants a carousel built around a framework they personally use.
test_cases.prompt: Help me create a LinkedIn carousel about the 5-step process I use to evaluate SaaS tools for my team. The goal is to build authority and get people to save it for reference.
expected_outputs: Asks for the actual 5 steps (and audience/voice) before drafting, OR drafts with clearly stated placeholder assumptions for the steps
Produces slide-by-slide copy: a hook slide, one slide per step, and a CTA slide
Hook is specific to evaluating SaaS tools, not generic
Names the framework so it is memorable and save-able
Final slide CTA fits the 'build authority + get saves' goal
Provides a ready-to-post caption on the topic
success_criteria: Delivers a concrete slide-by-slide carousel about SaaS evaluation (not advice about making carousels)
Pulls in (or asks for) the user's actual 5 steps and real evaluation criteria
Hook promises specific value to someone choosing SaaS tools
One idea per slide, tight copy, 5-10 slides — applied silently
Does NOT recite LinkedIn engagement statistics at the user
Caption is written out and on-topic

test_cases.name: Contrarian Carousel — produce the argument
test_cases.description: User wants a contrarian carousel challenging conventional wisdom.
test_cases.prompt: I want to post a LinkedIn carousel arguing that daily posting actually hurts engagement, not helps it. How do I structure this to get people commenting and engaging?
expected_outputs: Asks for the user's evidence/experience behind the claim, or what makes them credible on it
Produces slide copy that builds the argument: claim -> why people believe the opposite -> the user's evidence -> the counterintuitive truth -> what to do instead
Hook is a provocative, specific claim (not 'engagement tips')
CTA invites disagreement/comments, matching the goal
Provides a caption that frames the debate
success_criteria: Delivers actual slide copy that makes the contrarian case about posting frequency
Argument is built from the user's reasoning/evidence, not generic assertions
Hook is pointed and specific to the claim
Structure builds tension toward a payoff and a comment-driving CTA
Uses comment-driving craft silently, without lecturing about why contrarian posts drive comments
Does NOT pad with engagement benchmarks

test_cases.name: Personal Narrative — produce the story arc
test_cases.description: User wants to turn a personal story into a carousel with universal lessons.
test_cases.prompt: I left a $200K job to start a startup. I want to create a carousel about the unexpected lessons I learned. Will this format work well, and how should I structure it?
expected_outputs: Briefly confirms the format fits, then asks for the actual unexpected lessons and key story beats
Produces a narrative arc in slide copy: hook (the leap) -> story beats -> the surprising lessons -> what it means for the reader -> CTA
Hook centers the surprising outcome/decision
Helps generalize the personal lessons so they are useful to readers
Provides an authentic, on-topic caption
success_criteria: Delivers actual narrative slide copy built from the user's real story and lessons
Hook is specific and emotionally compelling about leaving the job
Lessons are concrete and made transferable to the audience
Voice reads personal/authentic, matching a first-person story
Narrative arc is coherent and lands a takeaway + CTA
Does NOT recite engagement statistics

test_cases.name: Design & Technical Question
test_cases.description: User has content and asks a direct technical/design question.
test_cases.prompt: I've outlined my carousel but I'm using Canva. What dimensions should I use, and what's the right way to export it for LinkedIn? Any design rules I should follow?
expected_outputs: Answers directly: 1080 x 1350px portrait, PDF export, key design rules
Concise and practical Canva-specific guidance
Does not bury the answer in engagement statistics
success_criteria: Gives the specific, correct answer (portrait 1080x1350, PDF Standard, fonts/contrast rules)
Stays concise and actionable for a Canva user
Here a direct spec answer IS on-topic — but does not pad with unrequested benchmarks or carousel-performance lectures
Offers to help apply the rules to the user's actual deck

test_cases.name: Pre-Publication Review of the user's deck
test_cases.description: User has a finished carousel and wants it reviewed.
test_cases.prompt: I've created my carousel on the 5-C framework for positioning. Before I post, can you review it and tell me if it meets best practices? I have 9 slides, headlines are specific, and design is consistent.
expected_outputs: Asks to see the actual headlines/slide content so the review is real, not generic
Reviews the user's specific deck against craft standards (hook strength, one idea per slide, density, CTA, save-ability)
Gives targeted, specific feedback on THEIR content, not a recital of rules
Confirms what is working and flags concrete improvements
success_criteria: Requests or works from the user's actual slide content
Feedback is specific to the 5-C positioning deck, not a generic checklist dump
Evaluates hook, per-slide focus, density, and CTA on their material
Validates craft (9 slides is fine, etc.) without reciting the underlying statistics
Offers concrete rewrites where slides are weak

test_cases.name: Weak Hook Diagnosis
test_cases.description: User reports poor engagement and shares their hook.
test_cases.prompt: My carousel about LinkedIn tips only got 50 impressions. The first slide just says 'LinkedIn Tips for Success' with a swipe arrow. Why didn't it perform?
expected_outputs: Identifies the generic hook as the likely primary cause, engaging with their actual hook text
Explains why 'LinkedIn Tips for Success' fails to earn a swipe
Rewrites the hook into 2-3 specific alternatives tailored to their topic
Suggests a simple way to test the improvement
success_criteria: Diagnoses the user's specific hook, not hooks in the abstract
Provides concrete rewritten hook options for their content
Explains the 'earn the swipe' principle plainly without citing engagement percentages
Gives a practical retest suggestion

test_cases.name: Text Wall Diagnosis
test_cases.description: User has text-heavy slides and low completion.
test_cases.prompt: I have great content about my sales methodology but each slide has about 100 words. People aren't finishing. What's wrong?
expected_outputs: Identifies text density as the core problem for their specific case
Explains the readability/skim principle plainly (no stat-padding required)
Shows how to split their dense slides into more, tighter ones
Optionally demonstrates by rewriting one of their 100-word slides into 2-3 tight slides
success_criteria: Diagnoses text walls as the cause and engages with their sales-methodology content
Gives a concrete restructuring plan (split content, one idea per slide, ~30 words)
Demonstrates with an actual rewrite of their material where possible
Explains the 'why' in plain terms without reciting completion-rate statistics

test_cases.name: Timing & Posting Question
test_cases.description: User is ready to post and asks how/when.
test_cases.prompt: My carousel is ready to go live on LinkedIn. When should I post it? What's the step-by-step process for uploading to LinkedIn?
expected_outputs: Gives a specific timing recommendation (Tue/Wed, late morning) concisely
Provides the step-by-step LinkedIn document-upload workflow
Includes a short caption pointer if helpful
Stays practical; does not lecture with benchmark statistics
success_criteria: Answers the actual question: specific timing + clear numbered upload steps
Workflow is correct and complete (Start a post -> Document -> upload PDF -> title -> caption -> Post)
Concise and practical; timing rationale kept brief, not a stats dump
Here specific timing IS the on-topic answer — but it is not padded with unrelated benchmarks

test_cases.name: Performance Diagnosis & Next Steps
test_cases.description: User reports a result and wants to know what to improve.
test_cases.prompt: My carousel got 2% engagement rate. How does that compare to benchmarks? What should I focus on improving for my next carousel?
expected_outputs: Gives useful context on whether 2% is low for their situation (the user explicitly asked for the comparison, so a benchmark here is on-topic)
Asks diagnostic questions about THEIR carousel (hook, density, CTA, audience size)
Prioritizes concrete improvements for their next post
Does not turn the answer into a generic statistics lecture beyond what was asked
success_criteria: Answers the comparison the user asked for, then pivots to actionable diagnosis
Asks about or reasons over the user's specific carousel to find likely causes
Gives prioritized, concrete next steps (improve hook, cut text, clarify CTA)
Benchmark is offered because the user asked — not volunteered as padding elsewhere

test_cases.name: Any-topic content (non-business)
test_cases.description: Proves the skill creates good content for any subject, not just business/marketing topics, and personalizes it.
test_cases.prompt: Make me a LinkedIn carousel about how I got into trail running and what it taught me about consistency.
expected_outputs: Runs a short discovery round: the user's actual trail-running story, the consistency lessons, audience, tone, goal — or states assumptions and drafts
Produces slide-by-slide copy about THE USER'S trail-running journey and lessons
Hook is specific to their story, not 'lessons on consistency' in the abstract
Generalizes the lessons so a professional audience finds them relevant
Provides an on-topic caption and a fitting CTA
success_criteria: Carousel is genuinely about trail running + consistency, using the user's story
Does NOT drift into LinkedIn/carousel meta-advice
Content is specific and personal, not interchangeable filler
Applies craft (length, tight slides, hook, CTA) silently
Asks for the user's real details or clearly flags assumptions before drafting

test_cases.name: Thin brief — discovery, not a stat dump (anti-pattern guard)
test_cases.description: A one-line request that should trigger discovery questions, not an immediate generic deck or a lecture about carousel best practices.
expected_outputs: Asks the discovery questions first: topic, the user's credibility/specifics, audience, voice, goal
Does NOT immediately produce a generic carousel
Does NOT respond with a lecture of LinkedIn engagement statistics or carousel best practices
Frames the questions as a quick, easy-to-answer round
success_criteria: Leads with a focused discovery interview rather than guessing
No carousel about 'how to make carousels' is produced
No engagement-benchmark recitation
Questions are grouped and efficient, not a one-by-one interrogation

coverage_areas: Content creation on the user's topic (carousels 001, 002, 003, 010)
Review of the user's own deck (carousel 005)
evaluation_focus: Produces ready-to-build carousel CONTENT about the user's actual topic
Personalizes to the user's voice, audience, expertise, and goal
Runs discovery before drafting (or states assumptions)
Diagnoses the user's specific content when troubleshooting
Does NOT recite LinkedIn engagement statistics at the user (anti-pattern)
